definition: Resentful means full of bitter indignation at being treated unfairly — nursing the sting of a wrong done to you and letting it color how you act.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word resentful. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know resentful should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Omar grew resentful of the weekend shifts that somehow always landed on him, saying nothing at the meetings but shutting the schedule drawer a little harder each Friday.
Annoyed is far milder than resentful: annoyance flares at an inconvenience and fades by dinner, while resentful means the sense of being wronged has settled in to stay.
Embittered goes further than resentful: a resentful person still nurses one particular wrong, but an embittered one has been soured all the way through, until the bitterness outlives its causes.

Bitter is the broader, harder word — a person can turn bitter about life itself, with no single wrong left to point to. Resentful stays aimed: it smolders at a particular unfairness and at whoever dealt it, and it can still fade once the wrong is put right.

Aggrieved means feeling wronged, often with a formal edge — the aggrieved party in a lawsuit has a stated injury. Resentful adds the brooding: not just registering the wrong but nursing it, replaying it, letting it sour every later dealing.

Passed over for the solo she had rehearsed all winter, the second violinist turned resentful: she still played every note beautifully, but she stopped sharing her bowings with the newcomer and left the hall the moment rehearsal ended.
Nothing erupts here — no shouting, no scene.

Resentful names the quieter injury: the settled, smoldering sense of having been treated unfairly, aimed at a particular wrong and at whoever dealt it, and leaking out in withheld favors and early exits rather than open anger.
Resentful is the adjective for a person still carrying a wrong: it takes of, at, or toward, and the grammar wants a culprit — you are resentful of the decision, at the committee, toward the favorite.
Keep it apart from envious, which merely wants what another has; resentful believes something was taken or denied unfairly.
And where rancor (also in this unit) names the old, banked bitterness itself, resentful describes the person the bitterness lives in while it is still warm.

For eleven years the Aldana and Reyes farms shared an irrigation ditch, and for eleven years Marta Aldana believed the water board had shorted her side.
The 2014 ruling gave the Reyes fields first draw every July, the very month her peppers needed it most, and she was never told why.
Her neighbors called her resentful, and she did not argue.
She waved at the Reyes truck and kept her fences neat, but she skipped the harvest supper every year and voted against anything the family proposed.
It was not the town she was angry at, and not farming; it was one decision, and the board that had made it without a word to her.
Last spring a new clerk found the error — a surveyor's transposed digit — and redrew the schedule.
By August, Marta was hosting the supper herself.
